lessonTitle: Stroke and Transient Ischaemic Attack: Localisation, Imaging and Secondary Prevention

blocks.text: A 69-year-old woman is cooking when she suddenly cannot find words, her right arm goes limp and her mouth droops on one side. Her husband calls an ambulance. Within the hour a doctor must decide whether she has a clot or a bleed, because the same drug that could restore her speech would be dangerous if the cause is haemorrhage. Time is brain, and the examination tells you where the damage is.

blocks.markdown: A **stroke** is a sudden focal neurological deficit of vascular origin lasting more than 24 hours or causing death; a **transient ischaemic attack (TIA)** is a transient deficit from focal ischaemia without infarction on imaging (the tissue-based definition), usually resolving within an hour. Most strokes (about 85%) are **ischaemic**, from large artery atheroma, cardioembolism (atrial fibrillation is the commonest source) or small vessel disease; the rest are **haemorrhagic** (intracerebral haemorrhage and subarachnoid haemorrhage). The brain has high metabolic demand and no reserve, so about 2 million neurones are lost each minute in a large vessel occlusion; the ischaemic **penumbra** around the core can be salvaged if blood flow is restored quickly.

rows: Contralateral weakness and sensory loss of face and arm more than leg; homonymous hemianopia; dominant hemisphere: aphasia; non-dominant: neglect
Total anterior circulation syndrome has all three of: hemiparesis, hemianopia, higher cortical dysfunction
Contralateral leg weakness more than arm; abulia, urinary incontinence
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing

Vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, dysarthria, crossed signs, reduced consciousness; lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, contralateral body pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome, dysphagia
Brainstem and cerebellum; basilar occlusion can be fatal
Pure motor, pure sensory or sensorimotor stroke, without cortical signs
Internal capsule, thalamus, pons; linked to hypertension and diabetes
blocks.caption: Stroke syndromes by vascular territory (Bamford/OCSP classification groups them as TACS, PACS, LACS and POCS).

blocks.title: Localising a stroke
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old man has sudden left face and arm weakness, left-sided visual field loss on both eyes' left halves, and does not acknowledge his left arm. Which vessel is affected?

steps.text: Left-sided motor and sensory deficit involving face and arm points to the right cerebral hemisphere (contralateral).
Left homonymous hemianopia is a right hemisphere optic radiation or occipital deficit, and neglect of the left side is a non-dominant (right) parietal sign.
Weakness of face and arm, plus hemianopia and neglect, is a total anterior circulation pattern, so the right middle cerebral artery (or its terminal ICA).

blocks.answer: Right MCA territory infarct (total anterior circulation syndrome).

blocks.title: Why image first
blocks.text: Clinical examination cannot distinguish ischaemic from haemorrhagic stroke. Non-contrast CT head is performed immediately to exclude intracranial haemorrhage before any thrombolytic is given, because thrombolysis causes bleeding. Imaging also excludes stroke mimics (such as tumour or subdural haematoma); hypoglycaemia is excluded by a glucose check.

blocks.markdown: **Imaging decisions.** *Thrombolysis* (intravenous alteplase or tenecteplase) is given for ischaemic stroke within 4.5 hours of onset (or last known well), after CT excludes haemorrhage and contraindications such as recent surgery, anticoagulation with a raised INR or very high blood pressure are checked. Beyond 4.5 hours, or in wake-up stroke, advanced imaging (MRI or CT perfusion) can identify salvageable penumbra. *Thrombectomy* (mechanical clot retrieval) is considered for proximal large vessel occlusion (for example the internal carotid or proximal MCA), which is shown by CT or MR angiography, and may be offered up to 24 hours in selected patients with perfusion imaging showing salvageable tissue; it is usually combined with thrombolysis if eligible. Imaging therefore answers three questions: is it a bleed, is there a large vessel to retrieve, and is there tissue still worth saving.

blocks.title: Weight-based alteplase dose
blocks.prompt: Teaching example: alteplase is dosed at 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg), 10% as an IV bolus and the remainder infused over 60 minutes. Calculate the total dose, bolus and infusion for an 80 kg patient.
blocks.answer: 72 mg total: 7.2 mg bolus then 64.8 mg infused over 60 minutes (teaching example only; check against current BNF, NICE and local thrombolysis guidance).

blocks.title: Grading carotid stenosis
blocks.prompt: A patient with a left hemisphere TIA has an internal carotid artery whose narrowest point is 2.0 mm and distal normal ICA diameter is 5.0 mm. Calculate the stenosis.

steps.text: Form the ratio of narrowest to distal normal diameter.
Stenosis is one minus the ratio, as a percentage.
A symptomatic stenosis of 50 to 99% (NASCET) benefits from carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of the event.

blocks.answer: 60% symptomatic stenosis: refer promptly for carotid endarterectomy.

items: Antithrombotic therapy: antiplatelet after ischaemic stroke or TIA once haemorrhage is excluded. For acute ischaemic stroke, NICE advises aspirin 300 mg daily for 2 weeks, then long-term clopidogrel 75 mg daily; for TIA, clopidogrel 75 mg daily is the usual first choice. Check against current NICE NG128, BNF and local protocols, which vary.
Cardioembolic stroke with atrial fibrillation: anticoagulation (usually a direct oral anticoagulant) rather than antiplatelet, started at a time dictated by infarct size.
Statin therapy for lipid lowering, and blood pressure reduction once the acute phase has passed.
Carotid endarterectomy for symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50 to 99%.
Lifestyle and risk factors: stop smoking, reduce alcohol, exercise, weight loss, manage diabetes.

points: Stroke localisation follows the vascular territory: MCA (face and arm, language or neglect, hemianopia), ACA (leg), PCA (hemianopia), posterior circulation (vertigo, crossed signs), lacunar (pure motor or sensory).
CT is needed before thrombolysis to exclude haemorrhage; CT angiography identifies large vessel occlusion for thrombectomy; perfusion imaging identifies salvageable tissue.
Secondary prevention: antithrombotic therapy, statin, blood pressure control, anticoagulation in AF, carotid surgery when indicated, and lifestyle change.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has sudden weakness of the left face, arm and leg of equal severity. Speech, vision, cognition and sensation are normal. Which stroke syndrome is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pure motor deficit without cortical signs in a patient with hypertension and diabetes.
distractorRationale.b: A total anterior circulation stroke also has hemianopia and higher cortical dysfunction.
distractorRationale.c: Lateral medullary syndrome causes crossed sensory loss, vertigo and Horner syndrome.
distractorRationale.d: PCA infarction causes visual field loss, not hemiparesis.

questions.explanation: Equal face, arm and leg weakness without aphasia, neglect, hemianopia or sensory loss is a pure motor lacunar syndrome, typically from small vessel occlusion in the internal capsule or pons. Hypertension and diabetes are its main risk factors.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing and a left-sided Horner syndrome. He has loss of pain and temperature on the left side of the face and the right side of the body. Where is the lesion?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain and temperature loss, Horner and bulbar signs.
distractorRationale.b: An internal capsule lesion causes contralateral motor or sensory loss without crossed signs.
distractorRationale.c: Occipital lesions cause visual field loss.
distractorRationale.d: A frontal lesion would not cause crossed brainstem signs.

questions.explanation: Crossed sensory loss arises because the spinal trigeminal nucleus (ipsilateral face) and the spinothalamic tract (contralateral body) are both damaged in the lateral medulla. Horner syndrome and bulbar weakness complete the picture of lateral medullary syndrome, usually from vertebral or PICA occlusion.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman suddenly cannot see objects to her right side in either eye. Power, sensation and speech are normal. Which territory is involved?

options.text: Left middle cerebral artery with aphasia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: right homonymous hemianopia from left occipital cortex infarction.
distractorRationale.b: ACA infarct causes contralateral leg weakness.
distractorRationale.c: Left MCA would also cause weakness and aphasia.
distractorRationale.d: Right MCA would cause left-sided deficits.

questions.explanation: Isolated homonymous visual field loss with preserved motor and sensory function localises to the occipital cortex supplied by the posterior cerebral artery. Right visual field loss arises from the left hemisphere.

questions.stem: Why must a non-contrast CT head be performed before giving intravenous thrombolysis to a patient with suspected stroke?

options.text: To exclude intracranial haemorrhage, which thrombolysis would worsen
To measure the infarct size accurately within minutes

questions.correctOptionText: To exclude intracranial haemorrhage, which thrombolysis would worsen

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke look the same clinically.
distractorRationale.b: Early CT is insensitive to infarct size.
distractorRationale.c: AF is diagnosed by ECG, not CT.

questions.explanation: The clinical picture cannot distinguish infarct from haemorrhage, and thrombolysing a haemorrhage would increase bleeding. CT also identifies some stroke mimics.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman has had an ischaemic stroke and her ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which approach to secondary prevention is most appropriate once the acute phase has settled?

options.text: Anticoagulation, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant, plus a statin and blood pressure control
No treatment because the stroke has occurred

questions.correctOptionText: Anticoagulation, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant, plus a statin and blood pressure control

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cardioembolic stroke is best prevented by anticoagulation.
distractorRationale.b: Antiplatelets are less effective than anticoagulants for AF.
distractorRationale.d: Endarterectomy is for symptomatic carotid stenosis only.

questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes left atrial thrombus and cardioembolism, so anticoagulation reduces recurrence more than antiplatelet therapy. Statin and blood pressure control address the atherosclerotic risk.

questions.stem: A man was last known to be well at 10:20. At 13:35 his CT shows no haemorrhage. Taking the standard thrombolysis window as 4.5 hours from last known well, calculate how many minutes remain until the window closes.
questions.explanation: The window is 270 minutes. From 10:20 to 13:35 is 195 minutes, so 270 - 195 = 75 minutes remain. Decisions on thrombolysis and on CT angiography for thrombectomy need to be made in parallel and quickly.

questions.stem: After a right-sided TIA a carotid angiogram shows an internal carotid artery narrowest diameter of 1.2 mm and a distal normal ICA diameter of 5.0 mm. Calculate the NASCET percentage stenosis.
questions.explanation: Stenosis = (1 - 1.2/5.0) x 100 = (1 - 0.24) x 100 = 76%. A symptomatic stenosis of 50 to 99% warrants carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of the event.

questions.stem: Explain why imaging is needed before decisions about thrombolysis and thrombectomy, and what each type of imaging contributes.
markingGuide: Clinical features cannot distinguish ischaemic stroke from haemorrhage
Non-contrast CT excludes haemorrhage, a contraindication to thrombolysis
CT also excludes mimics such as tumour
CT or MR angiography identifies proximal large vessel occlusion suitable for thrombectomy
Perfusion imaging or MRI shows salvageable penumbra versus core beyond the standard window
Thrombolysis window 4.5 hours from onset or last known well
Thrombectomy for proximal occlusion, often combined with thrombolysis
questions.explanation: Reperfusion treatments help ischaemia but harm haemorrhage, so the first question is bleed or clot. Angiography and perfusion imaging then show whether a large vessel can be retrieved and whether brain tissue is salvageable.

questions.stem: Describe the secondary prevention measures after an ischaemic stroke due to large artery atherosclerosis.
markingGuide: Antiplatelet therapy (after ischaemic stroke: aspirin 300 mg for 2 weeks then long-term clopidogrel 75 mg per NICE; after TIA: clopidogrel usually first choice; check current NICE NG128 and local protocols)
Blood pressure control after the acute phase
Carotid imaging and endarterectomy for symptomatic stenosis 50 to 99%, ideally within 2 weeks
Smoking cessation, exercise, diet, glycaemic control
questions.explanation: Recurrence is highest early, so prevention targets thrombus formation, atheroma progression and blood pressure. Surgical treatment of a tight symptomatic carotid stenosis removes the embolic source.

questions.stem: True or false: isolated contralateral leg weakness with abulia and urinary incontinence suggests anterior cerebral artery territory ischaemia.
questions.explanation: The leg and medial frontal lobe are supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, so infarction produces contralateral leg weakness and frontal features such as abulia and incontinence. MCA strokes affect face and arm more than leg.
